pages.title: The retrieval layer is the moat, not the model
pages.breadcrumb: Insights > Applied AI & Generative AI > The retrieval layer is the moat, not the model
pages.seo_title: The retrieval layer is the moat, not the model | Applied AI
pages.meta_description: Foundation models are converging on capability; the durable advantage sits in retrieval, permissions and freshness.

blocks.x: Foundation models are converging on capability; the durable advantage sits in retrieval, permissions and freshness.
The argument

The retrieval layer is the moat, not the model is not a slogan; it is a delivery position. The evidence is consistent across industries — the constraint is rarely technology; it is whether the operating model takes this seriously from sprint one.
Three things that matter

items: Point 1
Every enterprise answer should cite its source paragraph — provenance is the feature that survives audit.
Point 2
Permission-aware retrieval turns your existing entitlements into AI guardrails for free.
Point 3
Freshness SLAs on corpora are the difference between trusted assistants and abandoned demos.

blocks.x: Three questions to ask your current vendors

items: Question 1
Where exactly does the evidence for each claim live — and can your auditor reach it without a project?
Question 2
Which named individual owns the control environment around this capability — not the function, the person?
Question 3
What did you stop last quarter, and what did the stop save us?

blocks.x: Where programs fail with this

Programs stall when the operating model is treated as an afterthought — the technology works in week six and the organization has not changed in week sixty, so the capability quietly degrades into shelfware.
What we do differently

items: Gate the enthusiasm
falsifiable criteria and locked baselines before build; the demo is the least important artifact.
Design the operating model
named owners, run models and escalation paths agreed with the operating team, not for it.
Generate evidence in-flight
replay trails, control tests and documentation as artifacts of the build — never reconstructed.

blocks.x: The number that matters
Grounded-answer rates above 92% are achievable when retrieval is engineered, not appended.

pages.breadcrumb: Insights > Applied AI & Generative AI > GenAI unit economics: the metric nobody tracks
pages.seo_title: GenAI unit economics: the metric nobody tracks | Applied AI
pages.meta_description: Cost per resolved task — not per token — is the real unit of GenAI economics.

blocks.x: Cost per resolved task — not per token — is the real unit of GenAI economics.
The argument

GenAI unit economics: the metric nobody tracks is not a slogan; it is a delivery position. Across engagements the pattern repeats: programs that respect this move faster and survive audit; those that do not pay for it later — usually in the audit itself.
Three things that matter

items: Point 1
Routing across model tiers cuts cost 40-60% at equal task quality on most workloads.
Point 2
Distillation to right-sized models converts frontier quality into commodity cost.
Point 3
Caching and prompt discipline matter more than model choice for high-volume flows.

blocks.x: Three questions to ask your current vendors

items: Question 1
What is the classical baseline every proposed capability must beat, measured on identical data?
Question 2
Who signs the go/no-go gate, and what evidence do they require before signing?
Question 3
What did you stop last quarter, and what did the stop save us?

blocks.x: Where programs fail with this

The argument

Retrofit first, rip-and-replace never is not a slogan; it is a delivery position. We keep seeing the same economics: teams that internalize this spend their budget on value, while teams that ignore it spend on rework and explanations.
Three things that matter

items: Point 1
Protocol translation (fieldbus → OPC UA/Sparkplug) is the unglamorous heart of every twin.
Point 2
Calibration and data contracts make telemetry trustworthy enough for models.
Point 3
Ex-rated environments need Ex-rated engineering — safety discipline precedes sensing.

blocks.x: Three questions to ask your current vendors

items: Question 1
What is the classical baseline every proposed capability must beat, measured on identical data?
Question 2
Which named individual owns the control environment around this capability — not the function, the person?
Question 3
Show us a negative result you documented — the discipline is the product.

blocks.x: Where programs fail with this

The failure mode is predictable: enthusiasm funds the demo, budget cycles gate the industrialization, and by the time the governance conversation starts, shadow usage has already created the exposure the review was meant to prevent.
What we do differently

items: Gate the enthusiasm
falsifiable criteria and locked baselines before build; the demo is the least important artifact.
Design the operating model
named owners, run models and escalation paths agreed with the operating team, not for it.
Generate evidence in-flight
replay trails, control tests and documentation as artifacts of the build — never reconstructed.

blocks.x: The number that matters
Critical assets get instrumented with near-zero production downtime using non-invasive mounting.

blocks.x: One crying-wolf quarter kills the program; alarm governance is a first-class design goal.
The argument

Predictive maintenance fails socially before it fails statistically is not a slogan; it is a delivery position. Across engagements the pattern repeats: programs that respect this move faster and survive audit; those that do not pay for it later — usually in the audit itself.
Three things that matter

items: Point 1
Failure-mode-driven models beat generic anomaly detection — physics before ML.
Point 2
Predictions must become work orders with parts reserved, or they are dashboard decorations.
Point 3
Planner trust (share of predictions actioned) is the KPI that predicts program survival.

blocks.x: Three questions to ask your current vendors

items: Question 1

Question 2
Who signs the go/no-go gate, and what evidence do they require before signing?
Question 3
What did you stop last quarter, and what did the stop save us?

The argument

The twin is a decision instrument, not a 3D screenshot is not a slogan; it is a delivery position. Across engagements the pattern repeats: programs that respect this move faster and survive audit; those that do not pay for it later — usually in the audit itself.
Three things that matter

items: Point 1
Physics + data hybrids validate against measured reality — or the twin is fiction.
Point 2
Configuration governance recalibrates when the asset changes; drift monitoring keeps it honest.
Point 3
Scenario engines (what-if, sensitivity) are where planners actually live.
